lesson.title: Bundling Data and Behavior: An Introduction to Object-Oriented Programming
lesson.summary: Object-oriented programming groups related data and the functions that operate on it into a single unit called an object, instead of keeping data and behavior as separate pieces you have to pass around together by hand.
lesson.body:
So far, data and the functions that work on it have mostly lived apart. A dictionary holds a dog's name and breed, and a separate function takes that dictionary as an argument to do something with it, like producing a greeting. Nothing is wrong with this approach for small programs, but as programs grow, you end up passing the same handful of related values into function after function, and nothing in the code enforces that a "dog dictionary" actually has the keys a function expects.

```python
dog_data = {"name": "Rex", "breed": "Lab"}

def bark(dog):
    return f"{dog['name']} says Woof!"

print(bark(dog_data))
```

```
Rex says Woof!
```

This works, but the connection between dog_data and bark is informal. Nothing stops you from calling bark on a dictionary that has no "name" key, and every new behavior you want a dog to have becomes another loose function that has to be told which dictionary to work on. Object-oriented programming, OOP for short, is a different way of organizing code that ties data and behavior together on purpose, into a single unit called an object. A dog object would carry its own name and breed and also its own bark behavior, all bundled together, so you never have to remember to pass the right data to the right function.

This is really an extension of an idea you have already used: abstraction, hiding the messy details behind a clean interface, and functions, packaging a chunk of behavior under one name you can call. OOP takes both ideas further by letting you package behavior together with the specific data it acts on, and by hiding exactly how an object stores its data behind the methods it exposes. The blueprint for what an object looks like is called a class, and a specific object built from that blueprint is called an instance. The next several concepts unpack exactly how to write a class, how to build objects from it, and how each object keeps track of its own information, starting with what a class actually is.
